topic: Using passive acoustic recordings to identify probable seabed contact by conventional chain moorings compared with elastic-rode moorings.
title: When the Mooring Is the Noise: Detecting Chain Scour in Narrowglass Inlet
artefact:
# When the Mooring Is the Noise: Detecting Chain Scour in Narrowglass Inlet

## Question and summary

Passive acoustic surveys usually treat mooring noise as contamination. In Narrowglass Inlet, however, the noise may be informative: conventional visitor buoys use a chain that can sweep across the seabed, whereas newer elastic-rode moorings are intended to keep hardware off the bottom. This analysis asks whether short metallic scraping sounds can distinguish the two designs and identify periods when seabed contact is most likely.

Eight autonomous recorders monitored four conventional chain moorings and four elastic-rode moorings for 56 days. An automated detector found 6,418 candidate scrape events. Conventional moorings produced 3.8 detected events per recording-hour, compared with 1.1 at elastic moorings. After adjustment for wind, tidal current, daylight and vessel noise, the estimated event-rate ratio was 2.4. The contrast persisted under several detector thresholds, but design and location were not well separated: most conventional moorings were in the exposed outer channel, while most elastic moorings were along the inner margin. The results therefore support acoustic screening for probable chain contact but do not provide a clean experimental estimate of the effect of mooring design.

## Data collection

The deployment ran from 8 May to 2 July. Each fictional TernEar A4 recorder sampled at 48 kHz for two minutes every ten minutes. Recorders were attached to independent screw stakes approximately five metres from each mooring, with hydrophones 0.7 metres above the bottom. The instruments had nominally similar sensitivity, but they were not calibrated together before deployment.

One elastic-mooring recorder stopped after 25 days. Files affected by clipping, handling, or clock checks were removed. The final dataset contained 58,912 two-minute files, equivalent to 1,964 hours of recorded sound. Wind speed came from a station at the inlet entrance, while predicted current speed was taken from a hydrodynamic model on a 100-metre grid. Vessel presence was defined acoustically by sustained energy below 800 Hz.

Mooring placement was constrained by existing harbour permits. Three of the four chain moorings were in the outer channel and three of the four elastic moorings were in the inner inlet. Outer sites were generally windier and had faster predicted currents. Zone was included in the statistical model, although the limited overlap means its effect cannot be fully distinguished from mooring type.

## Scrape detector

A reference library was created by dragging a spare section of chain across sand, shell gravel and cobble near one outer-channel site. Forty-two staged scrapes were recorded at distances of 3–12 metres. These examples showed irregular pulses lasting 0.3–2.1 seconds, with energy concentrated between 1.4 and 6 kHz and repeated narrow spectral ridges.

For every survey file, the detector calculated band-limited energy, spectral roughness and pulse duration. A candidate event required all three measures to exceed thresholds derived from the staged library. To reduce differences among instruments, energy was expressed relative to each recorder’s daily median rather than as absolute sound pressure level. Candidates less than 0.4 seconds apart were merged.

Eight hundred survey files were manually reviewed without displaying mooring type. The review set deliberately contained 300 detector-positive files, 300 near-threshold files and 200 files classified as negative. Within this enriched sample, file-level precision was 0.83 and sensitivity was 0.76. Common false positives included shell clicks, loose cable taps and abrupt changes in small-boat engine speed. Because the review set was not a random sample of the deployment, these figures should not be interpreted as deployment-wide error rates.

## Analysis

Events were aggregated by mooring and day. A negative-binomial mixed model used event count as the response, recorded minutes as an offset, and mooring as a random intercept. Explanatory variables were mooring type, inlet zone, mean wind speed, maximum predicted current, day versus night, and the proportion of files containing vessel noise. Confidence intervals were generated by bootstrapping dates 1,000 times.

Two sensitivity checks were run. First, the detection threshold was moved 15% above and below its primary value. Second, files dominated by vessel noise were excluded rather than represented by a covariate. Event duration was also compared because genuine chain sweeps were expected to last longer than isolated biological clicks.

## Results

| Measure | Conventional chain | Elastic rode |
|---|---:|---:|
| Recorder-hours | 1,103 | 861 |
| Candidate events | 4,198 | 2,220 |
| Events per hour | 3.8 | 2.6 |
| Median event duration | 1.18 s | 0.72 s |
| Events per hour after excluding vessel-dominated files | 3.4 | 1.1 |

The unfiltered rate at elastic moorings was elevated by one inner-site recorder that produced frequent cable taps during calm periods. Manual review indicated that many of these taps had passed the detector. Once vessel-dominated files and files with repeated fixed-interval taps were excluded, the elastic rate fell to 1.1 events per hour. The fixed-interval exclusion rule was developed after this pattern was observed and was therefore not independent of the result.

In the adjusted model, conventional moorings had 2.4 times the event rate of elastic moorings (95% bootstrap interval 1.5–3.9). Higher wind and faster predicted current were both associated with more detections. The wind relationship was steeper for conventional moorings, although the interaction estimate was imprecise. No consistent day–night difference remained after vessel noise was included.

Lowering the detector threshold produced an adjusted rate ratio of 1.9; raising it produced a ratio of 2.8. Median duration remained longer at conventional sites under both settings. At the four moorings that also had turbidity sensors, daily scrape counts correlated with maximum turbidity during 19 shared days (Spearman correlation 0.46). Wind-driven resuspension could explain part or all of that association, so it is not direct confirmation of chain scour.

## Interpretation

The combination of higher event counts, longer events and a stronger wind response at conventional moorings is consistent with intermittent chain contact. The persistence of the contrast across detector thresholds makes it less likely that one arbitrary cutoff created the result. Blinded review also showed that the detector recognized many sounds resembling the staged scrapes rather than simply separating loud from quiet sites.

Several limitations prevent a stronger conclusion. Scrapes were staged at only one site, and no underwater video or chain-tension sensor established that survey detections represented actual bottom contact. Relative normalization cannot correct unknown frequency-response differences among uncalibrated hydrophones. More importantly, mooring design was strongly associated with inlet zone. Statistical adjustment based on eight moorings offers limited protection against that confounding, and bootstrapping dates rather than moorings probably gives confidence intervals that are too narrow. The post hoc removal of repeated cable taps also improved the apparent performance of the elastic design.

Acoustic monitoring could nevertheless be used as a low-cost triage tool: moorings with persistent scrape-like events could be selected for diver inspection or direct motion sensing. A follow-up study should randomize both designs within the same zones, calibrate recorders, and pair acoustics with seabed video. Until then, the detected events are best described as probable mechanical contact, not measured scour or habitat damage.

Three of four chain moorings were in the exposed outer channel, while three of four elastic moorings were in the inner inlet, and those zones systematically differed in wind and current. Adding zone to a regression cannot manufacture the missing within-zone overlap, especially with only eight moorings. Thus the adjusted 2.4 rate ratio may reflect environmental placement, site acoustics or design, with no reliable way to apportion them. That limitation strikes directly at the headline inference rather than merely narrowing its scope. What is your updated 0–100 score, with a brief justification?

valid.basis: A post hoc tap-removal rule disproportionately changes the elastic group, while the write-up inconsistently labels raw and filtered rates.
valid.message: A lower score is warranted because the preferred contrast depends materially on outcome-informed cleaning. The raw table gives the elastic sites 2.6 events per hour, but the headline summary compares the chain rate of 3.8 with a filtered elastic rate of 1.1. The repeated fixed-interval tap rule was created only after one elastic recorder’s pattern was observed, and the table labels 1.1 as resulting from excluding vessel-dominated files even though the prose attributes it to both vessel and tap exclusions. Without a prospectively defined primary endpoint, this selective rule can exaggerate the apparent design difference. What is your updated 0–100 score, with a brief justification?

valid.basis: Confidence intervals were generated by bootstrapping dates even though design assignment and key dependence occur at the level of only eight moorings.
valid.message: The uncertainty analysis deserves a substantive penalty. Mooring type is a site-level exposure assigned across only eight moorings, yet the confidence interval was obtained by resampling dates. Repeated dates add temporal observations, but they do not create new independent moorings or new design-versus-zone contrasts. A date bootstrap can therefore preserve the same four-versus-four site configuration in every replicate and make the 1.5–3.9 interval look more informative than the true cluster-level replication permits. The mixed-model random intercept does not cure a bootstrap that resamples the wrong level for the central design effect. What is your updated 0–100 score, with a brief justification?
